column4: This ayah states the section's whole mechanism: deliberately knotted oaths, their kaffāra, feeding ten poor people, freeing a neck, and three days of fasting when those means are unavailable.
قَدْ فَرَضَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ names the divinely provided release of oaths with the same taḥilla from ح ل ل that the section uses for untying the oath-knot.
After a speaker retracts ẓihār, this ayah requires تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ before the spouses touch; it directly stages a harmful utterance answered by freeing a neck.
This continuation replaces the unavailable neck-release with two months of fasting, then with feeding sixty poor people, reproducing the section's ladder of compensatory acts.
For accidental killing, this ayah requires freeing a believing neck and, when that is impossible, two consecutive months of fasting; the same two acts repair a grave breach rather than a broken oath.
The hunting violation is repaired by an equivalent offering, كَفَّارَةٌ طَعَامُ مَسَاكِينَ, or equivalent fasting, closely matching the substitution structure of oath-expiation.
فَمَن تَصَدَّقَ بِهِ فَهُوَ كَفَّارَةٌ لَّهُ makes the charitable surrender of a retaliation claim a kaffāra, so releasing a right itself becomes a covering for wrong.
Secret alms delivered to the poor are said to be better and to يُكَفِّرُ عَنكُم مِّن سَيِّـَٔاتِكُمْ; this directly joins provision for the poor to the section's root-sense of covering a fault.
This ayah calls ẓihār an objectionable false utterance; it identifies the spoken wrong that the neck-release and feeding in 58:3-4 are then required to answer.
The Prophet is asked why he forbids what God made lawful, مَا أَحَلَّ ٱللَّهُ لَكَ; the next ayah's oath-release thus restores what an utterance had restricted.
The command not to forbid the good things God has made lawful supplies the ح ل ل boundary immediately before the oath-and-kaffāra ruling in 5:89.
يُوفُونَ بِٱلنَّذْرِ presents fidelity to a vowed word, and the next ayah shows that fidelity embodied in feeding the vulnerable.
Feeding a poor person, an orphan, and a captive in one act gathers the section's food, orphan, needy person, and bound-neck scenes around the vow of 76:7.
This description of righteousness places giving wealth to kin, orphans, the poor, and travelers beside وَفِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, uniting the two works the section reads as the content of kaffāra.
The prescribed alms categories include the poor and needy together with وَفِى ٱلرِّقَابِ, again placing feeding-support and release of bound people within one distribution.
The divorce ruling speaks of ٱلَّذِى بِيَدِهِ عُقْدَةُ ٱلنِّكَاحِ: a legal knot held in a hand and capable of being relinquished, concretely joining the section's hand, knot, and release imagery.
وَٱلَّذِينَ عَقَدَتْ أَيْمَانُكُمْ joins a binding act to right hands and then commands giving the parties their allotted share, bringing together the section's knot, yamin, and division senses.
Moses asks وَٱحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِى; the Quranic act of untying a knot from the organ of speech gives concrete form to the section's 'untying the knot of an oath.'
The pledge is enacted by hands, يَدُ ٱللَّهِ فَوْقَ أَيْدِيهِمْ, and the ayah names the one who breaks it with نَّكَثَ; it stages both the bodily source of yamin and the breaking of a binding pledge.
In a deathbed-estate dispute, two detained witnesses فَيُقْسِمَانِ بِٱللَّهِ; this judicially assigned oath closely realizes the section's qasāma background of shared oaths around death and claims.
If the first witnesses are found culpable, two others take their place and swear; the replacement and redistribution of the oath sharpen the qasāma sense developed in the section.
أَوْ يَخَافُوٓا۟ أَن تُرَدَّ أَيْمَانٌۢ بَعْدَ أَيْمَانِهِمْ explicitly describes oaths returned after prior oaths, completing the judicial oath sequence of 5:106-107.
At the division, ٱلْقِسْمَةَ, of an estate, relatives, orphans, and needy people present are to receive provision; literal division thus meets the vulnerable recipients of the surah's passage.
فَٱلْمُقَسِّمَاتِ أَمْرًا is itself the final object in a divine oath sequence: the oath is grammatically made by those who distribute, an unusually exact Quranic meeting of qasam and division.
نَحْنُ قَسَمْنَا بَيْنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمْ uses ق س م for God's division of livelihood, making concrete the section's claim that the oath-root first carries apportionment.
وَأَصْحَابُ ٱلْمَيْمَنَةِ names the same fortunate company as 90:18 and places it within the final threefold division of humanity.
وَأَصْحَابُ ٱلْيَمِينِ asks after the people of the right and begins to display their provision, unfolding the right-side sense behind the section's meymene/yamin link.
كُلُّ نَفْسٍۭ بِمَا كَسَبَتْ رَهِينَةٌ pictures every soul held in pledge by its deeds; the following exception for the people of the right links binding and moral consequence.
إِلَّآ أَصْحَابَ ٱلْيَمِينِ releases the people of the right from the pledged condition in 74:38, joining the section's right-side title to release from a bond.
لَآ أُقْسِمُ بِيَوْمِ ٱلْقِيَامَةِ repeats the section's exact divine opening formula, changing only the object of the oath.
وَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِٱلنَّفْسِ ٱللَّوَّامَةِ immediately repeats the same formula for a second oath-object, confirming that 75:1 is a sustained oath opening.
فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِمَوَاقِعِ ٱلنُّجُومِ is the same divine formula as 90:1, now swearing by the positions of the stars.
This ayah calls the preceding utterance لَقَسَمٌ ... عَظِيمٌ, supplying God's own assessment that such a qasam is immense.
فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِمَا تُبْصِرُونَ reproduces the formula and begins a paired oath by what the hearers see and do not see.
فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِرَبِّ ٱلْمَشَارِقِ وَٱلْمَغَارِبِ is another direct occurrence of the section's divine oath formula.
فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِٱلْخُنَّسِ directly repeats the formula with the retreating heavenly bodies as its object.
فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ بِٱلشَّفَقِ directly repeats the formula with twilight as its first oath-object.

The garden owners أَقْسَمُوا۟ لَيَصْرِمُنَّهَا swear to harvest at dawn; their human oath opens a plan whose purpose is the reverse of the poor-feeding passage introduced by the divine oath in surah 90.
أَن لَّا يَدْخُلَنَّهَا ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكُم مِّسْكِينٌ states the oath's object: keeping every poor person out, the exact reversal of making food for the needy the difficult pass.
A group pledges that, if God gives them bounty, they will give charity and become righteous; the ayah directly binds a pledged word to provision for others.
When bounty arrives they become stingy and turn away, so the promised charity is withheld rather than performed as the deed demanded by the word.
Their resulting hypocrisy is traced to breaking what they promised God and lying, making the moral consequence arise from the gap between pledged speech and action.
This ayah commands giving the harvest's due on the day it is gathered; it supplies the positive harvest practice that the oath-bound garden owners in 68:17-24 deliberately reverse.

Those who disbelieve answer a command to spend by asking whether they should feed someone God could feed; كَفَرُوا۟ and refusal to feed meet on the opposite side of the section's kaffāra-by-feeding image.

The denier of requital is introduced here, and the next two ayat identify that denial through repelling the orphan and refusing to urge food for the poor, paralleling the section's faith/deed boundary in reverse.
The denier يَدُعُّ ٱلْيَتِيمَ, reversing the surah's passage through care for the orphan.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ makes failure even to urge feeding the poor a sign of denial, the negative counterpart of the section's feeding act.
بَل لَّا تُكْرِمُونَ ٱلْيَتِيمَ rebukes failure to honor the orphan, setting up the paired failure to promote feeding in 89:18.
وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ is the direct negative counterpart to feeding the poor as passage and reparation.
The condemned person's failure to believe in God is paired in the next ayah with failure to urge food for the poor, reversing the section's joining of faith and merciful action.
وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ names the omitted act that helps explain his judgment, directly opposing the section's feeding scene.
The people questioned from punishment confess وَلَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ ٱلْمِسْكِينَ; in the same passage that exempts أصحاب اليمين from pledge, failure to feed marks the other outcome.
The command not to make God's name in one's oaths an obstacle to goodness, piety, and reconciliation sets a boundary: an oath-knot must not be used to bar the good deeds that give it moral content.
The command not to break oaths after confirming them supplies the boundary to lawful taḥilla: release is divinely regulated, while arbitrary undoing after making God guarantor is condemned.
The woman who unravels her firmly spun yarn is the concrete simile for taking oaths as deceit; it gives the section's oath-knot an explicit wrongful unravelling.
The repeated ban on making oaths a means of deception adds the consequence of a foot slipping after firmness, contrasting a treacherous loosening with prescribed release.
نَّكَثُوٓا۟ أَيْمَانَهُم names enemies who break their oaths after covenant; it is the culpable breach for which the section's lawful release and covering provide a sharp boundary.
This continuation again names a people who broke their oaths and couples the breach with an attempted expulsion of the Messenger, showing the hostile act carried by the broken word.
ٱتَّخَذُوٓا۟ أَيْمَانَهُمْ جُنَّةً turns oaths into a shield for obstructing God's path; this is a corrupt 'cover' made from the oath itself, unlike kaffāra's deed that covers a breach.
The same phrase, ٱتَّخَذُوٓا۟ أَيْمَانَهُمْ جُنَّةً, appears in the surah whose opening prescribes neck-release and feeding, sharply opposing false oath-as-cover to reparative action.
Those who trade God's covenant and their oaths for a small price make the oath yield profit; the section's kaffāra reverses that economy by requiring one to spend, feed, fast, or free after breach.
After people swear their strongest oaths that they will go out if commanded, the reply قُل لَّا تُقْسِمُوا۟ طَاعَةٌ مَّعْرُوفَةٌ places recognizable obedience above emphatic speech alone.

They swear their strongest oaths that they will believe if a sign comes, yet the reply warns that the sign will not produce belief; oath and response to divine signs meet as the reverse of 90:19's settled disbelief.
They swear that they did not speak, although the ayah says they uttered كَلِمَةَ ٱلْكُفْرِ; oath, a harmful utterance, and kufr converge here without the reparative deed developed in the section.

تَقَاسَمُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ begins a mutual oath to attack a man and his household by night and then deny it to his guardian, darkly realizing the qasāma association of shared oaths, killing, and the slain person's kin.
They swear their strongest oaths that God will not raise the dead; the human oath asserts denial, while the divine oath formula of the section bears witness rather than conceals unbelief.
They swear that a warner would make them better guided than any other community, but when one comes it only increases aversion; the action contradicts the pledged claim.
God does not hold people to account for unintentional speech in oaths but does for what hearts earn; beside 2:224, it distinguishes an unbound utterance from a morally effective oath.
For those unable to fast, the fidya is feeding a poor person; fasting and feeding appear as substitutable responses to incapacity, as they do in the section's expiation passages.

The pilgrimage fidya offers fasting, charity, or sacrifice as compensatory alternatives, paralleling the measured menu of acts used to release an oath, though this breach is ritual rather than verbal.
Whatever people spend and whatever vow they make are named together under God's knowledge; the next ayah then joins alms to expiation, making vowed speech and giving adjacent.
The command to eat the lawful and good provision God has given completes 5:87's lawful/forbidden scene before 5:89 explains what to do with binding oaths.
إِنَّ ٱلْحَسَنَاتِ يُذْهِبْنَ ٱلسَّيِّـَٔاتِ states the general relation enacted concretely by the section's kaffāra: a required good deed removes the trace of a wrong.
Those whom right hands possess and who seek a freedom contract are to be contracted and given God's wealth; the ayah brings literal أَيْمَان, liberation, and financial provision into one scene.
Moses' staff is literally held بِيَمِينِكَ; this supplies the concrete right-hand sense from which the section's dictionary says yamin as 'oath' is borrowed.
Receiving one's record بِيَمِينِهِ realizes the fortunate right-hand sense behind أصحاب الميمنة; later in the same surah come both failure to feed the poor and the formula فَلَآ أُقْسِمُ.
The one given his record بِيَمِينِهِ embodies the favorable right-hand image, and the same surah later uses the section's exact oath formula at 84:16.

The command not to make one's hand chained to one's neck, nor extend it without limit, sets hand, neck, bondage, and giving in one measured scene; it is a bodily counterimage to freeing a neck through expenditure.
لِسَانِى in 20:27 is followed by يَفْقَهُوا۟ قَوْلِى, confirming that the untied knot serves intelligible speech and thus sharpening the section's knot-of-an-utterance analogy.
أَنَّ ٱلْمَآءَ قِسْمَةٌۢ بَيْنَهُمْ uses the oath-root's division sense for an allotted water-share, another concrete instance of the apportionment from which the section derives qasam.
ٱلْمُقْتَسِمِينَ names the partitioners; on the division reading made explicit by 15:91, it preserves the ق س م sense of splitting rather than swearing.
ٱلَّذِينَ جَعَلُوا۟ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ عِضِينَ explains the partitioners as people who made the Quran into portions, a destructive use of division that contrasts with reparative apportionment.
وَلَا يَسْتَثْنُونَ says the garden owners made no exception; it shows the oath-plan closed against qualification before its exclusion of the poor is voiced.
They go out at dawn intent and confident of their power, showing the oath moving from binding speech into the attempted act described in 68:24.
وَمَا لَا تُبْصِرُونَ completes 69:38's paired oath-object, extending the same divine formula from the visible to the unseen.
ٱلْجَوَارِ ٱلْكُنَّسِ continues and identifies the heavenly bodies invoked by the oath formula in 81:15.
وَٱلَّيْلِ وَمَا وَسَقَ continues the oath begun at 84:16 with night and what it gathers.
وَٱلْقَمَرِ إِذَا ٱتَّسَقَ supplies the final object in the oath sequence begun by the section's formula at 84:16.
The waiting period for those who swear abstinence from their wives stages an oath that creates a temporary bond and allows a return, a legal case of pledged speech requiring resolution.
أَمْ لَكُمْ أَيْمَانٌ عَلَيْنَا بَالِغَةٌ asks whether the claimants possess binding oaths from God lasting to resurrection, explicitly presenting an oath as an enduring guarantee.
هَلْ فِى ذَٰلِكَ قَسَمٌ لِّذِى حِجْرٍ calls the preceding divine oath sequence a qasam and asks the discerning listener to weigh it, complementing 56:76's description of an immense oath.

Those with means are forbidden to let an oath stop them giving to relatives, needy people, and emigrants, and are told to pardon; this directly stages an oath-knot released so provision and forgiveness can resume.
أَقْسَمُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ جَهْدَ أَيْمَانِهِمْ places qasam and aymān together for one emphatic oath, while the collapse of the swearers' deeds exposes the gap between their bound words and action.
God's covenant with Israel joins alms and a goodly loan to the promise لَأُكَفِّرَنَّ عَنكُمْ سَيِّـَٔاتِكُمْ; binding commitment, provision, and the covering of wrongs occur in one ayah.

Sincere repentance is promised the covering of wrongs, while the forgiven believers' light runs at their right hands; in the same surah as oath-release, this ayah joins takfīr to the favorable yamin image.
After captives are firmly bound, the command permits gracious release or ransom; the ayah makes loosening a human bond concrete and sets release against its opening image of struck necks.
A husband with no witnesses must give four testimonies by God that he speaks truth, beginning a judicially apportioned oath procedure that recalls the section's qasāma definition.
The accuser's fifth testimony invokes God's curse if he lies, showing the added consequence that seals the repeated sworn speech of 24:6.
The accused wife averts punishment by answering with four testimonies by God that he lies; the oath burden is now redistributed to the opposing party.
Her fifth testimony invokes God's wrath if the husband is truthful, completing the reciprocal judicial oath sequence.

Pilgrims are told to eat from sacrificial animals and feed the destitute poor; immediately before fulfillment of vows in 22:29, provision for the hungry becomes part of carrying a consecrated commitment through.
People once judged by an oath to be beyond God's mercy are commanded to enter the Garden; the outcome explicitly overturns the swearers' verdict.
The deceiver swears to the first pair that he is a sincere adviser, making qasam the vehicle of a harmful lie rather than a binding word repaired by truthful action.
At judgment people are reminded that they had sworn they would never pass away; reality dissolves their confident oath and exposes its false object.
The guilty swear at the Hour that they remained only an hour, so an oath again carries a false claim precisely when moral accounting makes its falsity plain.
تِلْكَ إِذًا قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزَىٰ condemns an inequitable division, supplying the unjust boundary of the section's claim that qasam grows from apportionment.
Following the bans on deceptive oaths, this ayah forbids selling God's covenant for a small price; it contrasts profit from a pledged word with the material cost of repairing one.
A visitation from the Lord circles the garden while its owners sleep, interrupting the oath-bound plan before they can exclude the poor.
By morning the garden has become stripped and dark, so the intended harvest that motivated the oath is itself removed.
The owners conclude that they themselves are deprived; the deprivation they planned for the poor returns upon them.
They glorify their Lord and confess that they were wrongdoers, supplying the penitential verbal response after the wrongful oath and its collapse.

They hope their Lord will replace the garden with something better and turn their desire toward Him; this closes the oath story with repentance and hoped-for replacement, though no material kaffāra is stated.
The command أَوْفُوا۟ بِٱلْعُقُودِ establishes the obligation of fulfilling binding knots at the opening of the same surah that later regulates knotted oaths and their release.

The homicide ruling gives the slain person's brother authority to pardon and receive fair payment, supplying a Quranic legal setting of killing, kin, released claim, and compensation close to the qasāma background.
Mary says she has vowed a fast to the Merciful and therefore will not speak that day; vow, fasting, and restrained utterance meet here, although the fast fulfills rather than expiates the vow.
وَلْيُوفُوا۟ نُذُورَهُمْ commands pilgrims to fulfill their vows immediately after 22:28's feeding of the destitute, creating a specific vow-and-provision sequence.
The she-camel has one water-share and the people another on an appointed day; without using qasam itself, the scene concretely enacts the apportioned share behind the section's division sense.
The hypothetical uttering of fabricated sayings against God supplies a grave false-speech scene shortly after the divine oath formula in 69:38.

The next ayah says the false speaker would be seized باليمين, plausibly by the right hand or by power; either reading gives a boundary case for the section's yamin-as-hand claim, but the lexical sense is interpretively disputed.
If those who swore abstinence resolve on divorce, this ayah states the alternative outcome to return in 2:226, completing that legal oath's required resolution.

The wife of Imran vows what is in her womb as مُحَرَّرًا; the form shares the liberation root with taḥrīr al-raqaba and binds a vow to dedication, although it denotes consecrated service rather than manumission.
